prime.problem: Without scoping questions and a numeric "how well" list, you design a paid, tiered, multi-floor system for a free one-floor lot, or a design that fits on a laptop for a service that must take 3,858 reads a second. And if you keep only summaries, tomorrow's question can't be answered.
prime.fits: First card of the framing part, and the source of the course's running numbers. Every later estimate (back-of-envelope, SLO arithmetic, the overview's formula) starts from the non-functional list written here.
expect: clarifying questions that change the design
prime.goal: Turn a one-line prompt into two requirement lists with numbers on the second, and push a new feature through the three-question check.

attend: Which of the source's clarifying questions (levels, vehicle types, push vs pull, paid vs free, tiers) changes both lists, and why?
How do 100M new links a month turn into 38.6 writes/s and 3,858 reads/s, and which assumption hides in the 30-day month?
Why can a click counter never answer "clicks by country", while raw click rows can?
What does the primary key on links.code turn from a requirement into?
Where does the card say the functional/non-functional split is blurry, and what does raw data cost at TinyURL scale?

must: Functional list (what it does) → decides what to build; non-functional list as numbers (how well) → decides which design survives → features alone fit on a laptop, the numbers show why that fails
Clarifying questions → each answer changes one or both lists (one floor vs five, pushed vs pulled data) → asking first prevents designing for the wrong system
Store only a summary → the raw events are gone → any question not planned for (clicks by country) needs an ingestion change and loses history; store raw rows → new reports come from old data
Raw data has a price (10,000,000,000 click rows a month here) and privacy rules may cap retention → keep raw events in cheap storage for a fixed period and serve reads from summaries built from them
elevated: A database constraint (PRIMARY KEY on the code) → the "codes are unique" requirement is enforced by the engine, not by hope → a duplicate fails loudly (UNIQUE constraint failed)
reference: the five -ility definitions word for word
the sqlite3 schema and SQL text

compress.prompt: From memory, write the TinyURL requirement sheet as two short columns, with numbers on the second. Then write the three feature-check questions and one sentence on why raw data beats a counter.
checklist: functional: shorten, redirect, track clicks, accounts
non-functional with numbers: 38.6 writes/s, 3,858 reads/s, 3 TB in 5 years, never lose a mapping
ask clarifying questions first, because the answers change the lists
feature check: changes scope? non-functional impact? raw data to support it?
summaries lose the ability to answer new questions; raw rows cost storage and privacy

retrieve.q: Explain why a TinyURL design built only from its four features can look correct and still fail, and which list exposes the failure.
answer: four features fit a single dict on one machine
only the non-functional numbers (3,858 reads/s, 3 TB, never lose a row) rule that design out
the non-functional list, as numbers, is what picks the design

retrieve.q: Trace the source's 3-question check for "custom aliases": what does each question return, and what already makes it cheap?
answer: 1: yes, the user picks the code
2: one uniqueness check per write, at 38.6 writes/s: a primary-key lookup
3: yes, the links table already holds every code

retrieve.q: Product wants raw click rows kept forever "just in case". Give the cost at the card's scale and the compromise the card suggests.
answer: 100 clicks per new link → 10,000,000,000 rows a month
compliance may limit how long per-user events can be kept
keep raw events for a fixed retention in cheap storage and serve reads from summaries built from them

retrieve.q: For the financial dashboard, why does "all stocks with open > N and close < M" force a decision about raw data before any design is drawn?
answer: the filter needs each bar's open and close together
an average close can't answer it
so the storage must keep one row per price bar

compare.q: Both cards compute TinyURL's 38.6 writes/s and 3 TB. What is each card doing with the same numbers, and which mistake does each one prevent?
answer: here the numbers are requirements: they define "how well"
there they are inputs to a feasibility check with overheads and Little's law
requirements prevent building the wrong thing; estimation prevents building something that can't fit

compare.q: cs-5's image-resize card turns a requirement into cores and machines. Where does this card's work stop and that card's start, and what goes wrong if you start there without this card?
answer: this card fixes the rate and the targets
that card divides the rate by per-core work and leaves headroom
without a scoped rate and target, the sizing chain has no trustworthy input

predict.q: Keep every TinyURL input but change the read:write ratio from 100:1 to 1,000:1. Which numbers on the sheet change, and which stay exactly the same? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: Only the read rate changes: 38.58 × 1,000 ≈ 38,580 reads/s. Writes stay 38.6/s, records stay 6,000,000,000 and storage stays 3 TB, because storage is driven by new links, not reads. The design pressure moves entirely to the read path (caching, replicas), which is why the ratio is a clarifying question worth asking.

apply.task: Write the requirement sheet for an illustrative paste-sharing site: 10M new pastes a month, 10:1 reads to writes, 10 KB per paste, kept 1 year, 30-day months. List 4 functional and 4 non-functional requirements, compute the rates and storage, then run "syntax highlighting per language" through the three-question check.
apply.done: Your sheet shows about 3.86 writes/s, 38.6 reads/s and 1.2 TB for a year, each non-functional line has a number or a named rule, and the feature check has an answer for all three questions.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: which numbers move when only the read ratio changes?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the second list must carry numbers?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: clarifying question → which list changes, or raw data → which future feature it enables?
Could you argue both sides of "keep raw clicks" in an interview in under a minute?
What will you carry into the back-of-envelope card?
